summary: This module covers the fundamentals of Electrical Transformers. It introduces the definition, working principle, and static nature of transformers, explaining why they operate at high efficiencies with minimal maintenance. It details the three major components: primary winding, magnetic core, and secondary winding, along with the concepts of mutual induction, useful core flux, and leakage flux. The constructional aspects of the laminated silicon steel core are explored, highlighting how laminations suppress eddy current losses and silicon steel minimizes hysteresis loss. Furthermore, it presents the comprehensive classification of transformers (core-type vs. shell-type, step-up vs. step-down, power vs. distribution, autotransformers, and instrument transformers) and concludes with the theoretical characteristics and governing relations of an ideal transformer.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Define a transformer and explain why it is referred to as a 'static machine'.
sa.a:
A transformer is a static AC machine that transfers electrical energy from one electric circuit to another without any change in frequency, operating on the principle of electromagnetic induction between two or more magnetically linked circuits.

It is called a 'static machine' because it has no moving or rotating mechanical components. Consequently, it has zero mechanical losses (no friction or windage loss), requires minimal maintenance, and exhibits exceptionally high efficiency (typically 96% to 99%).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the working principle of a transformer and mention the two fundamental physical phenomena it relies on.
sa.a:
A transformer operates on the principle of mutual induction between two stationary windings linked by a common magnetic flux.

It is based on two fundamental physical phenomena:
1. Electromagnetism: An alternating electric current passing through the primary winding produces a time-varying magnetic field.
2. Electromagnetic Induction (Faraday's Law): The time-varying magnetic flux linking the secondary winding induces an electromotive force (EMF) across its terminals, transferring energy without electrical connection.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between 'useful flux' (main flux) and 'leakage flux' in a transformer.
sa.a:
1. Useful Flux (Main Flux): The portion of the alternating magnetic flux produced by the primary winding that remains confined within the magnetic core and links both the primary and secondary windings. It is solely responsible for transferring energy between circuits.

2. Leakage Flux: The portion of the magnetic flux that strays into the surrounding air or insulation and links only one of the windings without linking the other. It produces leakage reactance and causes internal inductive voltage drops.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Why is the magnetic core of a transformer laminated and made of silicon steel?
sa.a:
1. Silicon Steel: Made of high-grade alloy containing 3% to 4.5% silicon. Silicon increases the electrical resistivity of the steel, significantly reducing eddy current losses and keeping the hysteresis loop narrow (reducing hysteresis loss).

2. Laminated Construction: The core is assembled from thin sheets (laminations of 0.35 mm to 0.5 mm thickness) insulated from each other by varnish. Lamination breaks up the path of circulating eddy currents into small loops, drastically reducing eddy current heating losses (which are proportional to the square of lamination thickness).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the four key assumptions or characteristics of an Ideal Transformer.
sa.a:
The four characteristics of an ideal transformer are:
1. Zero Winding Resistance: Primary and secondary windings have zero electrical resistance (R1 = 0, R2 = 0), meaning zero copper loss (I²R = 0).
2. Zero Magnetic Leakage Flux: 100% of the flux produced is confined to the core and links both coils (no leakage reactance).
3. Zero Iron/Core Losses: Zero hysteresis and zero eddy current losses in the core.
4. Zero Magnetizing Current: The core has infinite permeability, requiring negligible current to set up magnetic flux.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between Step-up and Step-down transformers.
sa.a:
1. Step-Up Transformer: Secondary voltage is higher than the primary voltage (V2 > V1, N2 > N1). Consequently, secondary current is lower than primary current (I2 < I1). Used at generating power stations to raise voltage for transmission.

2. Step-Down Transformer: Secondary voltage is lower than primary voltage (V2 < V1, N2 < N1). Consequently, secondary current is higher than primary current (I2 > I1). Used in distribution substations and electronic appliances to provide safe consumer voltages.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Compare Core-Type and Shell-Type transformers in terms of construction and flux path.
sa.a:
1. Core-Type Transformer: The windings surround/encircle a major part of the magnetic core. It has two limbs and a single magnetic circuit path. Low-voltage winding is placed inside next to the core, and high-voltage winding is placed outside.

2. Shell-Type Transformer: The magnetic core surrounds/encloses the windings. It has three limbs (two outer limbs and one central limb). The magnetic flux divides equally into two parallel paths through outer limbs (each carries Φ/2). The windings are placed on the central limb.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What is an Autotransformer? State its main advantage and disadvantage compared to a two-winding transformer.
sa.a:
An Autotransformer is a transformer that consists of a single continuous winding wound on a laminated magnetic core, part of which acts as the primary and part (or whole) acts as the secondary.

- Advantage: Requires substantially less copper, has smaller physical dimensions, lower cost, higher efficiency, and superior voltage regulation.
- Disadvantage: Lacks electrical/galvanic isolation between primary and secondary circuits, making secondary equipment vulnerable to high-voltage hazards if a fault occurs.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between a Power Transformer and a Distribution Transformer.
sa.a:
1. Power Transformer: Used in transmission substations at generating stations and bulk receiving points. Rated above 200 kVA. It operates near full load continuously and is designed for maximum efficiency at or near 100% full load.

2. Distribution Transformer: Used in local distribution networks to feed end consumers. Rated up to 200 kVA. It operates under fluctuating loads throughout the day and is designed for maximum 'all-day efficiency' (maximum efficiency at 50% to 70% load).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What are Instrument Transformers? Name the two main types.
sa.a:
Instrument Transformers are specialized high-accuracy transformers used to step down high voltages and heavy currents to safe, standardized levels suitable for conventional measuring instruments and protection relays.

The two types are:
1. Current Transformer (CT): Steps down high line current for measurement using a standard 5A AC ammeter.
2. Potential Transformer (PT): Steps down high line voltage for measurement using a standard 110V AC voltmeter.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) With the aid of a neat schematic diagram, explain the construction and working principle of a single-phase transformer. (8 marks)
(b) Explain why a transformer cannot operate on a direct current (DC) supply. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Construction and Working of a Single-Phase Transformer:

1. Construction:
- A single-phase transformer consists of two insulated electrical coils (primary and secondary windings) wound on a common laminated ferromagnetic core.
- The primary winding is connected to an AC source (V1), and the secondary winding is connected to the electrical load (V2).
- The core is made of high-permeability silicon steel laminations (0.35 mm to 0.5 mm thick) coated with insulating varnish to reduce core losses.

2. Working Principle:
- When an alternating voltage V1 of frequency f is applied to the primary winding, it draws an alternating current I1.
- This current produces an alternating magnetic flux (Φ) in the core according to Ampere's law.
- The magnetic core provides a low-reluctance path that channels the flux to link with both windings.
- Self-Induced EMF: The alternating flux links the primary turns N1, inducing a self-induced EMF E1 = -N1(dΦ/dt) that opposes the applied voltage (Lenz's Law, back EMF).
- Mutually Induced EMF: The same alternating flux links the secondary turns N2, inducing a mutually induced EMF E2 = -N2(dΦ/dt) at the same supply frequency.
- When the secondary circuit is closed across a load, an alternating current I2 flows, delivering power to the load.
- Transformation Ratio: E2 / E1 = N2 / N1 = K.

(b) Why a Transformer Cannot Operate on a DC Supply:
- A transformer functions solely on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, which requires a rate of change of magnetic flux (dΦ/dt).
- When connected to a DC source, the current is constant (unidirectional and steady). Therefore, the magnetic flux produced in the core is constant (dΦ/dt = 0).
- Consequently, no back EMF (E1) is induced in the primary winding to oppose the applied voltage.
- The primary winding impedance is reduced strictly to its very small ohmic resistance (R1).
- By Ohm's law (I = V / R1), an enormous current will flow through the primary coil, causing severe overheating and burning out the winding within seconds.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Classify transformers based on: (i) Core construction, (ii) Voltage transformation, (iii) Purpose/Application, (iv) Windings, and (v) Insulation/Cooling. (8 marks)
(b) Compare Core-Type and Shell-Type transformers with neat diagrams showing magnetic flux paths and winding arrangements. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Comprehensive Classification of Transformers:
1. Based on Core Construction:
   - Core Type: Windings surround the magnetic core; single magnetic circuit.
   - Shell Type: Core encloses the windings; double parallel magnetic circuit.
2. Based on Voltage Conversion:
   - Step-Up Transformer: Secondary voltage > Primary voltage (V2 > V1, N2 > N1).
   - Step-Down Transformer: Secondary voltage < Primary voltage (V2 < V1, N2 < N1).
3. Based on Purpose / Application:
   - Power Transformer: Used in transmission systems; rated > 200 kVA; designed for maximum efficiency at full load.
   - Distribution Transformer: Used in local supply; rated up to 200 kVA; designed for high all-day efficiency (50-70% load).
   - Isolation Transformer: 1:1 ratio used for electrical safety and noise decoupling.
   - Instrument Transformers: Current Transformer (CT) and Potential Transformer (PT) for measurement.
4. Based on Number of Windings:
   - Two-Winding Transformer: Separate, electrically isolated primary and secondary coils.
   - Autotransformer: Single continuous tapped winding; no electrical isolation.
5. Based on Insulation & Cooling:
   - Dry Type: Air-cooled (natural or forced); safe for indoor installations.
   - Oil-Immersed: Immersed in insulating mineral oil inside a steel tank for superior cooling and dielectric insulation.

(b) Comparison: Core-Type vs. Shell-Type Transformers:

Feature | Core-Type Transformer | Shell-Type Transformer
--------|-----------------------|-----------------------
Core Structure | Two vertical limbs and two horizontal yokes | Three limbs (central limb + two outer limbs)
Cross-sectional Area | Uniform across all limbs and yokes | Central limb area is TWICE that of each outer limb
Magnetic Flux Path | Single closed magnetic loop carrying full flux Φ | Two parallel magnetic paths, each carrying Φ/2
Winding Placement | Windings are wrapped around the two limbs | Both LV & HV windings are placed on the central limb
Insulation Placement | LV winding placed closest to core, HV wound over LV | Interleaved/sandwiched LV and HV coils
Mechanical Protection | Poor mechanical protection for windings | High mechanical protection against short-circuit forces
Repair & Maintenance | Easy to dismantle, inspect, and rewind | Relatively difficult to dismantle and repair
Applications | Preferred for high-voltage, large power ratings | Preferred for low-voltage, medium power ratings

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain the concept of an Ideal Transformer. State the four fundamental assumptions made and derive the transformation ratio. (6 marks)
(b) Discuss the various losses occurring in a practical transformer and explain how each loss is minimized by design and materials. (6 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Ideal Transformer & Derivations:
An ideal transformer is an imaginary, theoretical benchmark model with 100% efficiency and zero energy losses.

Four Core Assumptions:
1. Zero Winding Resistance: Primary and secondary windings have zero internal ohmic resistance (R1 = 0, R2 = 0). Thus, zero copper losses (I²R = 0) and terminal voltages equal induced EMFs (V1 = E1, V2 = E2).
2. Zero Magnetic Leakage: All magnetic flux lines are entirely confined within the core and link every turn of both coils.
3. Zero Core Losses: Zero hysteresis loss and zero eddy current loss in the magnetic core.
4. Infinite Core Permeability: Requires zero (or negligible) magnetizing current to establish the core flux.

Transformation Relationships:
- Induced EMF: E1 = 4.44 f N1 Φm, and E2 = 4.44 f N2 Φm.
- EMF per turn: E1 / N1 = E2 / N2 = 4.44 f Φm.
- Transformation Ratio: K = V2 / V1 = E2 / E1 = N2 / N1.
- Since efficiency is 100%, Input VA = Output VA:
  V1 * I1 = V2 * I2  =>  I1 / I2 = V2 / V1 = K.

(b) Losses in Practical Transformers and Their Mitigation:

1. Core Losses (Iron Losses, Pi):
- Hysteresis Loss (Ph): Caused by continuous reversal of magnetic domains in the core every half-cycle. Given by Steinmetz equation: Ph = η * Bm^1.6 * f * V.
  * Mitigation: Use high-grade silicon steel / CRGO steel having a very narrow hysteresis loop area.
- Eddy Current Loss (Pe): Caused by circulating currents induced in the core mass by alternating flux: Pe = K * Bm² * f² * t² * V.
  * Mitigation: Construct the core from thin insulated laminations (thickness t = 0.35 mm to 0.5 mm) coated with varnish.

2. Copper Losses (Ohmic Losses, Pcu):
- Caused by the electrical resistance of the primary and secondary copper windings: Pcu = I1² R1 + I2² R2.
  * Mitigation: Wind coils using high-conductivity electrolytic-grade copper with adequate cross-sectional area to minimize resistance.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain the constructional details of the transformer core, including the role of silicon steel and laminations. (6 marks)
(b) A 20 kVA, 2000/200 V, 50 Hz single-phase transformer has 66 turns on the secondary winding. Assuming an ideal transformer, determine: (i) Primary winding turns, (ii) Full-load primary and secondary currents, and (iii) Maximum value of magnetic flux in the core. (6 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Constructional Details of Transformer Core:
- The magnetic core provides a continuous, high-permeability, low-reluctance magnetic circuit to link the primary and secondary windings.
- Core Material: Constructed from cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) silicon steel containing 3% to 4.5% silicon. Silicon increases resistivity, cutting eddy currents and reducing hysteresis loss.
- Laminated Construction: Built using thin stamped laminations (typically 0.35 mm to 0.5 mm thick in 'E-I', 'L-L', or 'U-I' shapes). Laminations are coated with a thin layer of insulating lacquer or varnish.
- Stepped Core Cross-Section: In large transformers, rectangular core limbs waste space inside cylindrical coils. Stepped cruciform cores are used to maximize iron utilization and minimize copper length.

(b) Numerical Calculation:
Given Data:
- Rated Capacity = 20 kVA = 20,000 VA
- Primary Voltage, V1 = 2000 V
- Secondary Voltage, V2 = 200 V
- Frequency, f = 50 Hz
- Secondary Turns, N2 = 66 turns

(i) Primary Winding Turns (N1):
Transformation Ratio: K = V2 / V1 = 200 / 2000 = 0.1
N2 / N1 = V2 / V1
66 / N1 = 200 / 2000 = 0.1
N1 = 66 / 0.1 = 660 turns. (Ans)

(ii) Full-Load Primary and Secondary Currents:
- Rated Apparent Power S = V1 * I1 = V2 * I2 = 20,000 VA
- Full-load Primary Current I1 = 20,000 / V1 = 20,000 / 2000 = 10 A. (Ans)
- Full-load Secondary Current I2 = 20,000 / V2 = 20,000 / 200 = 100 A. (Ans)

(iii) Maximum Magnetic Flux in Core (Φm):
EMF Equation: E2 = 4.44 * f * N2 * Φm
For an ideal transformer, E2 = V2 = 200 V
200 = 4.44 * 50 * 66 * Φm
200 = 14,652 * Φm
Φm = 200 / 14,652 = 0.01365 Weber (Wb) or 13.65 mWb. (Ans)
